wine.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Kellerberg
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Kellerberg above Dürnstein: steep dry stone terraces of Gföhl gneiss facing south east, out of the westerly winds of the Ice Ages, so that patches of loess survive on the rock. The house takes the name from the baroque Kellerschlössl of Dürnstein.
wine.making: Picked by hand late in the autumn, as the Wachau DAC requires of every wine and the ripeness of a Smaragd asks. The codex of the Vinea Wachau forbids any enrichment of the must and allows a Smaragd no hint of oak, and the wine is fermented fully dry; the house speaks of as little intervention as it can manage in the cellar.
wine.glass: Mango, passion fruit and pineapple over ripe yellow peach and wet stone; dense and broad for a dry Riesling, with high extract, ripe acidity and an alcohol that reads as weight rather than heat, and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous on release, it is at its fullest after eight to ten years, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; decant a young bottle for an hour if it seems closed; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol, named for the emerald lizard.
The single vineyard; Austrian law asks for the word Ried before a vineyard's name.
The older form on the label, the Kellerberg of Dürnstein, before Ried was required.
The appellation since the 2020 vintage; its single vineyard wines are Grüner Veltliner or Riesling alone.

records.table: F.X. Pichler's Riesling Smaragd Ried Kellerberg grows on steep gneiss terraces above Dürnstein in the Wachau. Fully dry yet broad, with mango and ripe peach over stone, it carries the weight of the valley's ripest style, so pour it cool rather than cold.
records.story: In the middle of the nineteenth century, as the house tells it, a forebear of the family, a grower from Rohrendorf near Krems, moved into the Wachau, and a grandson bought land at Oberloiben, where the winery stood around the turn of the twentieth century. The F.X. of the name, a later grower of the family trained at the wine school of Krems, bought prized terraces early on and set out to show each site at the full ripeness of its grapes. In 1983 the growers of the valley founded the Vinea Wachau, with its codex against enrichment and its three styles of Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd, and F.X. Pichler stood with it from the beginning. Two years later a scandal over doctored sweet wines emptied Austria's export markets and brought a strict new wine law. The Riesling Kellerberg of 1990 was, by the house's own account, the wine that carried its name abroad, as the dry Smaragd wines of the Wachau led Austria's recovery. In 2009 the family moved into a new winery at Oberloiben, and since the 2020 vintage the Kellerberg has been a Ried of the Wachau DAC. To a sommelier the wine is the measure of how much ripeness a dry Riesling can carry.

others.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Loibenberg
others.note: Warmer and broader, from the hill above Loiben, the direct comparison with the Kellerberg.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Kellerberg
others.note: Grüner Veltliner at full Smaragd weight from the same terraces.

others.name: Unendlich
others.note: A selection of Riesling and of Grüner Veltliner made only in years the house judges fit; the name means endless.

traps: F.X. Pichler is not Rudi Pichler or Pichler-Krutzler: several unrelated Pichler estates work the Wachau, so read the initials.
Smaragd is a trademark of the Vinea Wachau, a growers' association, not a rank in Austrian law; it names ripeness, not the vineyard.
A Smaragd is dry: the word promises ripeness and weight, never sweetness.

cards.front: F.X. Pichler's Kellerberg: what rock lies under its terraces?
cards.back: Gföhl gneiss, a metamorphic rock, with patches of loess that the Ice Ages left on the sheltered south east slope.

cards.front: What does the word Smaragd on F.X. Pichler's Kellerberg label promise, and whose rule is it?
cards.back: A dry wine of at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol with no hint of oak, under the Vinea Wachau's own codex.

questions.q: A guest reads Smaragd on F.X. Pichler's Riesling Ried Kellerberg and expects a sweet wine. What do you tell them?

It is late picked and keeps some natural sugar

It is a dry wine aged a year in new oak
questions.exp: Smaragd is the Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, fermented dry to at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol; the codex allows it no hint of oak, so the new oak answer is wrong as well.

questions.q: By the house's own account, the Riesling Kellerberg of which vintage first carried the name of F.X. Pichler abroad?
questions.exp: The house dates its breakthrough abroad to the Kellerberg of 1990; 1983 is the founding of the Vinea Wachau, 1985 Austria's wine scandal and 2009 the house's new winery.

No source read here gave the vessels for the Kellerberg itself, so the making rests on the rules (hand picking under the Wachau DAC by Austrian Wine, no enrichment and no hint of oak under the Vinea Wachau's codex) and the house's own words on intervention; one German merchant's sheet that gives ten months in barrique was set aside, as it conflicts with the codex.

The forebear who came from Rohrendorf is described, not named, since his dates were found nowhere; the F.X. of the name and his son, who took the house over in 2018 by its own timeline, are living and are not named.
That F.X. Pichler served the Vinea Wachau from its beginning rests on the association's own anniversary page (Vinea Wachau: 30 Jahre Vinea Wachau), read through a search summary.
The name Kellerberg from the Kellerschlössl, which the house dates to 1787, is the house's account alone, so the year is not used.

wine.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Singerriedel
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Singerriedel, narrow terraces held by dry stone walls at the entrance to Spitz: shallow, sandy, meagre soil over paragneiss, with mica schist and bands of quartzite lower down; Riesling grows on the steep terraces and Grüner Veltliner at the foot.
wine.making: Picked by hand on the terraces late in the autumn, as the Wachau DAC requires and the ripeness of a Smaragd asks, with no enrichment under the Vinea Wachau's codex. The wine is fermented dry in stainless steel and in most vintages then rests in large wooden casks of several thousand litres, which give it no taste of oak.
wine.glass: Ripe yellow peach, apricot and lime zest over wet stone and a smoky note of the rock, with orange blossom; full and creamy yet dry, with firm acidity and a long, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Generous young, it settles after five years or so, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more, gaining honey and dried apricot.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if it seems tight; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol, named for the emerald lizard.
The single vineyard, the wall of terraces that rises at the entrance to Spitz.
The appellation since the 2020 vintage; every wine under it is picked by hand.

records.table: Franz Hirtzberger's Riesling Smaragd Ried Singerriedel grows on narrow dry stone terraces at the entrance to Spitz, in the western Wachau. Ripe peach and apricot over stone, full and creamy yet dry, it is a Riesling that rewards a decade in the cellar.
records.story: The Hirtzbergers are a family of growers at Spitz, in the western Wachau. The modern estate begins with the grower of the house who took over his parents' holding in 1948: by the account of the Vinea Wachau, he bottled its wine for the first time and picked out the terraces of single vineyards the family farms. In 1983 he was one of the growers who founded the Vinea Wachau, the association whose codex forbids enrichment and whose Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd measure the ripeness of a dry wine. His son took over the estate that same year, saw it through the wine scandal of 1985 and the strict law that followed, and led the association from 1988 to 2012, as the dry wines of the Wachau found their way abroad. The Singerriedel, the steep wall of terraces on paragneiss at the edge of the village, gave the house its signature Riesling, picked late for Smaragd and fermented dry. Since the 2020 vintage the vineyard has been a Ried of the Wachau DAC. In 2014 a son of the family founded a separate estate, the Weinhofmeisterei at Wösendorf, so a sommelier reads the whole name on the label: the Singerriedel of Spitz is Franz Hirtzberger's.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Honivogl
others.note: Grüner Veltliner of full Smaragd weight, ripe, powerful and dry, often named with the house beside the Singerriedel.

others.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Hochrain
others.note: A second single vineyard Riesling Smaragd of the house, from the Hochrain.

traps: The Weinhofmeisterei at Wösendorf, founded in 2014 by a son of the family, is a separate estate; Franz Hirtzberger is the house at Spitz.
Honivogl and Singerriedel are vineyard names, not producers.
Smaragd names the Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, never a sweet wine.

report: Founded is left empty: one account has the family buying its first vines at Spitz in the late nineteenth century and another speaks of a farm of the thirteenth century; no house page was found to settle it.

The grower of 1948 (born 1923, died 2007, by the Vinea Wachau's own notice) is described rather than named, as his dates rest on that one source; his son and grandson are living and are not named, and the brother who founded the Weinhofmeisterei in 2014 should be added to people.json by the read together agent (Mathias Hirtzberger).

The grower of 1948 as a founder of the Vinea Wachau in 1983 rests on the association's own notice and its fortieth anniversary release, which lists him among the founding fathers (the Sommelier Academy agrees); his first bottling is on the house's profile there, with no year given; the son's leadership from 1988 to 2012 rests on the Vinea Wachau's own notice, with Decanter calling him its long standing president.

The making rests on Falstaff's entries for several vintages (steel tank and large wooden barrel) and a merchant's listing that gives casks of three to five thousand litres; Falstaff lists steel alone for one vintage, so the record says most vintages.
The Ried Hochrain Riesling Smaragd is attested by Falstaff and a second listing only as a wine, so its note says nothing of the site.
The table and the ageing keep the library's view of a ripe, long lived Riesling; the region line's 'richest, most honeyed' is a judgement and is not repeated.

wine.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Schütt
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Schütt between Dürnstein and Unterloiben, partly terraced, on a fan of stream debris at the mouth of the Menthalgraben: deep, sandy and stony soil of weathered gneiss, poor in fine earth, so it drains fast.
wine.making: Picked by hand late in the autumn, as the Wachau DAC requires, with no enrichment under the Vinea Wachau's codex. The wine is fermented dry mostly in large, old oak casks, with some stainless steel beside them; the casks are big and old, so they give the wine air and texture rather than a taste of wood.
wine.glass: White pepper, green pear and quince over lentils and wet stone, with tobacco leaf as it ages; dense and savoury rather than fruity, dry and long, with a fine, stony grip.
wine.ageing: Reserved in youth and released later than most, it opens after five to eight years, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol, named for the emerald lizard.
The single vineyard, a fan of gneiss debris between Dürnstein and Unterloiben.
The baroque image of the saint on Knoll bottles since 1962, the house's own mark, not a seal.

records.table: Emmerich Knoll's Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Schütt comes from a stony fan of gneiss at Unterloiben and wears the baroque Saint Urban label. Peppery, savoury and dense, it is slow to open and long lived, so give it years and some air.
records.story: The Knolls have grown vines at Unterloiben, at the eastern end of the Wachau, since the early nineteenth century. By the house's account Knoll wine went into glass bottles from the 1950s, and in 1962 the baroque image of Saint Urban first appeared on the label, where it has stayed. In 1983 the growers of the valley founded the Vinea Wachau, whose codex forbids enrichment and whose Smaragd marks the ripest dry wine, and the Knoll wines carry its styles. After the wine scandal of 1985 and the strict law that followed it, the house kept its own pace: large old oak casks, late picking and a release later than most. From 1988 it added a Vinothekfüllung, a dry selection of late picked Grüner Veltliner made in nearly every year, joined by a Riesling in 2000. Its vineyards lie around the village, the Loibenberg, the Kellerberg and the Kreutles among them, with the Pfaffenberg across the border in the Kremstal, yet the house names the Schütt before them all. Since the 2020 vintage the Schütt has been a Ried of the Wachau DAC. A sommelier who pours it learns patience: it shows least on release and most a decade later.

others.note: Riesling from the same stony fan, slow to open and long lived.

Vinothekfüllung is a house term, not a legal or Vinea Wachau category.
The Saint Urban figure on the label is the house's own mark, not a regional seal.

report: The plan asked to confirm Ried Schütt or Ried Loibenberg: the house's own profile on the Vinea Wachau names the Schütt above all its sites, so the Schütt stands; the library names the Riesling of the Schütt as the house's most distinctive wine, and the Grüner Veltliner keeps two Grüner Veltliners in a group of three Rieslings, so no swap is proposed, though a checker may prefer the Riesling.
Founded is left empty: one account gives 1825 and another only the early nineteenth century, which is what the story says.
The bottles of the 1950s, the Saint Urban label of 1962 and the Vinothekfüllung of 1988 (Riesling from 2000) rest on the house's own profile on the Vinea Wachau, with SommSelect for 1962.

The large old oak casks with some steel rest on an importer's sheet (The Source Imports) and the Sommelier Academy; the sizes, the overnight settling and the avoided malolactic fermentation rest on the importer alone and are left out.
Left out for want of a second source: a new winery of 2014 joined to the old cellar by a tunnel, and a cousin's estate, the Loibnerhof.
The heads of the house of the last two generations are living and are not named; the house keeps its name.

wine.name: Riesling Zöbinger Heiligenstein Alte Reben
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the Kamptal DAC; Erste Lage, marked 1ÖTW, of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from old vines, a few of them planted before the Second World War.
wine.sites: The Zöbinger Heiligenstein above Zöbing, a bare hill of Permian sandstone and conglomerate with volcanic grains, its face held by dry stone terraces built by hand from the 1920s; part of the house's share is trained on the Lyra, a divided, lyre shaped trellis.
wine.making: The juice ferments in stainless steel at fifteen to twenty degrees Celsius, and the wine then rests on its lees, in steel and in large wooden casks, until bottling in the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Yellow peach, apricot and orange peel over smoke, warm stone and dried thyme; dry and firm, with fine, salty acidity, a silky weight and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Taut on release, it opens after five to seven years, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard on the sandstone hill above Zöbing; newer labels print Ried Heiligenstein.
Old vines: the house's old plantings on the Heiligenstein.
Erste Lage of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, a private classification outside the wine law.
The appellation since the 2008 vintage, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling above all.

records.table: Bründlmayer's Riesling Alte Reben comes from old vines on the Zöbinger Heiligenstein, the Kamptal's hill of desert sandstone above Zöbing. It is dry and firm, apricot and orange peel over smoke and warm stone, and it keeps for decades.
records.story: Bründlmayer is a family estate of Langenlois, in the Kamptal, whose Heurigen stands in a Renaissance vintner's house in the town. Its signature hill, the Heiligenstein above Zöbing, is usually said to appear in a monastic register of 1280 as Hellenstein, for the heat of its bare slope, before the name became Heiligenstein, the holy stone. From the 1920s dry stone terraces were built by hand on its face, and some of the vines on it lived through the Second World War. From 1979, as the son of the house took over from his parents, synthetic fertiliser was given up, by the house's own account; in time part of the hill was trained on the Lyra trellis, and a sparkling wine made in the bottle joined the range. In 1996 the Bründlmayers helped a new family to take over the running of Schloss Gobelsburg nearby. The Kamptal DAC followed with the 2008 vintage, and from 2010 the Traditionsweingüter, a private association of the Kamptal and Kremstal estates, ranked its members' sites, the Heiligenstein among its Erste Lagen. In 2015 the vineyards were certified organic. Alte Reben is the house's selection from its old vines on the hill: to a sommelier, Austrian Riesling grown on desert sandstone rather than on the Wachau's gneiss.

The Kamptal is not the Wachau: Smaragd, Federspiel and Steinfeder never appear on Bründlmayer's labels.
1ÖTW is the private mark of the Traditionsweingüter, not a rank in Austrian wine law.

report: Founded is left empty: one lexicon dates the family's tradition to 1581, but the house's own pages read here gave no year, so the story does not use it.
The register of 1280 and the name Hellenstein rest on the wein.plus lexicon and a wine wiki, both read through search summaries, and are told as what is usually said.

The making rests on the house's own factsheets: steel at fifteen to twenty degrees and lees until bottling in the summer for 2018, steel then a wooden cask of 2,500 litres for 2023 (bottled in February 2024); the record says many vintages and the year after the harvest.

The terraces of the 1920s, the vines that lived through the war, fertiliser given up in 1979, the Lyra and the organic certificate of 2015 are the house's own account; the son who took over around 1980 is living and is not named.
The Kamptal DAC of 2008 and the ÖTW ranking from 2010 are the library's; Austrian Wine confirms that 1ÖTW is a private classification outside the wine law.
The library names the sparkling wine Brut Reserve; the house's shop lists an Extra Brut Reserve, so the record uses that name.
Two of the house's Heiligenstein sheets disagree on vessels (2024 steel alone for the Riesling without the old vine selection, 2018 partly big casks), so the others line says nothing of the cellar.

wine.name: Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the Kamptal DAC; Erste Lage, marked 1ÖTW, of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter
wine.sites: The Lamm, on the south east foot of the Heiligenstein: deep loess and loam, the loam weathered from the hill's Permian sandstone and volcanic rock.
wine.making: Fermented and matured on its lees in large traditional casks of five thousand litres and more, made of Austrian oak from the Manhartsberg forest, a few of them new. Under the Kamptal DAC a single vineyard wine may not go for its state test number before April of the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, quince and yellow apple over white pepper, lentils and toasted hazelnut, with a hint of honey; broad, creamy and dry, with fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to drink on release, it gains depth over five to ten years, and a strong vintage keeps for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard of loess and loam at the foot of the Heiligenstein.
Erste Lage of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, a private classification outside Austrian wine law.
The appellation since the 2008 vintage, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling above all.

records.table: Schloss Gobelsburg's Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm grows in deep loess and loam at the foot of the Heiligenstein, on an estate tied to the monks of Zwettl since 1171. Broad and dry, pear, quince and white pepper, it is matured in large Austrian oak casks.
records.story: In 1171, as the house tells it, the Cistercian monks of Zwettl Abbey received their first vineyards in the Kamptal, on the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg. The castle of Gobelsburg passed through many noble families until 1740, when its last aristocratic owner sold it to the abbey, which already held an estate at Kammern nearby; in 1784 the two were joined as the wine estate of the Cistercian abbey of Zwettl. The monks ran the cellar themselves until 1995. In 1996 a family took over the running of the estate, with early help from the Bründlmayers of Langenlois, while the abbey kept the ownership. The new managers added a Tradition line, an ode to the cellar ways of Gobelsburg between 1800 and 1850. The Kamptal DAC came with the 2008 vintage, and the Traditionsweingüter, a private association of estates, ranked the Lamm and the Heiligenstein among its Erste Lagen. In 2021 the house marked eight hundred and fifty years of winegrowing. The Lamm is its fullest Grüner Veltliner: to a sommelier, a Kamptal wine of full weight from loess and loam, and a monastic estate's history in one glass.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Tradition
others.note: Made after the cellar ways of Gobelsburg between 1800 and 1850, in large casks of Manhartsberg oak.

others.name: Riesling Ried Heiligenstein
others.note: Riesling from the hill where the monks of Zwettl received their first vineyards in 1171.

traps: Gobelsburg is in the Kamptal, not the Wachau, so its labels never carry Smaragd, Federspiel or Steinfeder.
Tradition is a house range describing a method, not an Austrian legal category.
The monks of Zwettl ran the cellar until 1995; from 1996 a family ran the estate, so the wine is not made by monks.

cards.front: Schloss Gobelsburg's Lamm: what soil lies at the foot of the Heiligenstein?
cards.back: Deep loess and loam, the loam weathered from the hill's Permian sandstone and volcanic rock.

cards.front: Which abbey bought Schloss Gobelsburg in 1740, and since when had its monks held vineyards nearby?
cards.back: The Cistercian abbey of Zwettl; its monks received their first Kamptal vineyards, on the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg, in 1171.

questions.q: Schloss Gobelsburg's Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm carries 1ÖTW on its label. What does the mark mean?
opts: An Erste Lage of a private growers' ranking
A Grosse Lage in Austria's national wine law
The ripest dry style of the Vinea Wachau
A wine aged a full year before release
questions.exp: 1ÖTW marks an Erste Lage of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, a private classification outside the wine law; the ripest dry style of the Vinea Wachau is Smaragd, which a Kamptal wine never carries.

questions.q: In which year did the Cistercian abbey of Zwettl buy Schloss Gobelsburg from its last noble owner?
questions.exp: The abbey bought the castle in 1740; its monks had held vineyards nearby since 1171, its two estates were joined in 1784, and a family took over the running in 1996.

sources.title: Skurnik: Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm Erste Lage, Schloss Gobelsburg

report: Founded is the library's 1171, but by the house's own history 1171 is the year the monks of Zwettl received their first Kamptal vineyards, on the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg; the abbey bought the castle in 1740, so the plan's 'estate at Gobelsburg recorded from 1171' is loose.

The library's trap says the estate is run under lease by its winemaker; the house speaks of management by a family from 1996 with the abbey as owner, and no source read here gives a lease, so the record says the running of the estate.

The region's producers line has the Tradition wines made in old wooden casks moved on wheels, and the library has racking by the moon; neither was confirmed by any source read here, so the record says only an ode to the cellar ways of 1800 to 1850 (the house and Skurnik).
The casks of five thousand litres and more, a few new, rest on two importer notes for the 2019 and 2022 vintages; the Manhartsberg oak on the house's page and an importer.
The family that took over in 1996 and the couple of Bründlmayer who helped them are living and are not named.
The eight hundred and fiftieth year in 2021 rests on the house's jubilee edition and a wine travel page (Wine in Time).
